oauth.alternatives: Personal access tokens suit one user's own scripts, not many users.

appTypes.name: GitHub App (recommended)
appTypes.whenToUse: Default for agents. Fine-grained permissions, installer-picked repos, 8-hour user tokens with refresh. Exempt from org OAuth app restrictions.

appTypes.name: OAuth app
appTypes.whenToUse: Only for enterprise-level resources or all-repo access without an install. `repo` is full read and write. Org owners must approve it by default.

verdict.label: Self-serve, optional review
verdict.summary: GitHub does not review your app. Any user can install a public GitHub App. The deciding factor is the customer: an org owner must install it for org repos.
verdict.nextStep: Register a GitHub App at github.com/settings/apps/new with read-only Contents, Issues, and Pull requests.
verdict.customerSideGateNote: An org owner installs a GitHub App. A repo admin can instead if you request no organization permissions or Repository administration, unless the owner blocks it. OAuth apps need owner approval in new orgs.

composio.note: Composio provides managed OAuth for GitHub. Users see Composio on the consent screen, and you share its rate limit and default permissions. Bring your own GitHub App for your own name, permissions, or rate limit: add its client ID and secret to an auth config, and link users to your install page. Only new connections use the new auth config. Existing users keep theirs until they re-authenticate or you import their credentials.

stages.name: Prototype
stages.whoCanConnect: You and your own org. The app installs only on your account.
stages.notes: No review. A private GitHub App installs only on its owner account.

stages.name: Limited beta
stages.whoCanConnect: Any GitHub user. Org repos need an install by an owner or repo admin.
stages.notes: GitHub adds no wait. Each customer org may wait on its owner, with no timeline.

stages.name: Production
stages.whoCanConnect: Anyone on GitHub. Marketplace listing is optional.
stages.notes: No GitHub approval. Marketplace listings get a review with no stated timeline; your app works meanwhile. Paid plans need 100 installs and a verified publisher org.

scopeTiers.name: Sign-in and profile
exampleScopes: GitHub App with no repository permissions
scopeTiers.effect: No review and no org approval.

scopeTiers.name: Read repos, issues, and PRs
exampleScopes: OAuth: repo (no read-only option for private repos)
scopeTiers.effect: Org repos need an owner or repo admin install. OAuth apps must request `repo` (full read and write).

scopeTiers.name: Write: open issues, comment, push branches, open PRs
scopeTiers.effect: Write permissions show on the install screen. Security-minded orgs ask more questions.

scopeTiers.name: Background access (agent acts while the user is away)
exampleScopes: User token refresh (8 h access, 6 month refresh)
Installation token from your app's private key (about 1 h)
scopeTiers.effect: Rotate refresh tokens; each refresh kills the old pair. Installation tokens act as a bot without a user.

scopeTiers.name: Org administration
exampleScopes: Organization permissions such as Members or Administration
scopeTiers.effect: Only an org owner can install the app. Repo admins cannot.

requirements.item: A GitHub account (personal or organization) to own the app
requirements.detail: Use an organization if you may sell on Marketplace. Paid listings must be org-owned.

requirements.item: A unique app name, 34 characters or fewer

requirements.detail: A public repo or your account URL works if you have no site.
Add production and local URLs. Locally use 127.0.0.1, any port. Keep wildcard matching off.
Read-only where possible. Skip org permissions and Repository administration.

requirements.item: Private key and client secret stored as secrets
requirements.detail: The private key mints installation tokens. The client secret exchanges user codes.

requirements.item: Webhook URL and secret, or webhooks turned off
requirements.detail: Webhooks are on by default. Turn them off if you do not need events.
Required for Marketplace. Org owners check for them.

requirements.item: Verified publisher organization (paid Marketplace plans only)
requirements.detail: Also needs 100 installs and monthly and annual plans.

steps.title: Register a GitHub App
steps.detail: Open github.com/settings/apps/new, or for an org go to **Settings > Developer settings > GitHub Apps > New GitHub App**. Enter name, homepage URL, and callback URL. Keep **Expire user authorization tokens** checked, choose **Only on this account**, and click **Create GitHub App**. The settings page shows the App ID and Client ID.

steps.title: Choose minimal permissions
steps.detail: Set Metadata, Contents, Issues, and Pull requests to read. Add write only where the agent acts.

steps.title: Generate secret and private key
steps.detail: Click **Generate a new client secret** and **Generate a private key**. Store both in a secret manager.

steps.title: Build sign-in with PKCE
steps.detail: Redirect to https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize with client_id, redirect_uri, state, and an S256 code_challenge. Exchange the code with the code_verifier. Refresh before the 8-hour expiry.

steps.title: Install and test
steps.detail: Click **Install App** and choose selected repositories. Call `GET /user/installations` to confirm the token sees them.

steps.title: Make the app public
steps.detail: In **Advanced**, make the app public. GitHub does not review this.

steps.title: Handle install in onboarding
steps.detail: Call `GET /user/installations` after sign-in. If the org has no install, link to your install page or show the owner draft.

steps.title: Wait for org owners
steps.detail: Members and outside collaborators can request an install. The org owner decides. You cannot speed this up. Send the owner the draft message.

steps.title: Plan for rate limits
steps.detail: User tokens share 5,000 requests per hour across the user's apps. Installation tokens get up to 12,500, or 15,000 on Enterprise Cloud. Keep content creation under about 80 per minute.

steps.title: Publish privacy and support pages
steps.detail: Link both from the app description.

steps.title: Optional: list on Marketplace
steps.detail: Add description, logo, screenshots, pricing (free works), and privacy and support links. Click **Request publish**. Paid plans need a verified publisher org and 100 installs.

steps.title: Wait for Marketplace decision
steps.detail: Only if you listed. An onboarding expert contacts you. No stated timeline.

blockers.symptom: Org users see **Request** instead of **Install**, or your agent sees no org repos.
blockers.cause: Org permissions or Repository administration block repo admin installs.
blockers.fix: Drop those permissions, or send the owner the approval draft.

blockers.symptom: An OAuth app works for personal repos but not org repos.
blockers.cause: OAuth app access restrictions are on by default in new orgs.
blockers.fix: Ask the user to request owner approval, or switch to a GitHub App, which is exempt.

blockers.cause: The redirect_uri does not match a registered callback URL.
blockers.fix: Register the exact URL (up to 10), or omit redirect_uri to use the first.

blockers.symptom: Refresh fails with bad_refresh_token, or users are logged out.
blockers.cause: Refresh tokens rotate and break if reused or unused for 6 months.
blockers.fix: Save each new refresh token atomically; on failure, re-run sign-in.

blockers.symptom: Stored tokens stop working after users reconnect many times.
blockers.cause: GitHub keeps at most 10 tokens per user, app, and scope, revoking the least recently used.
blockers.fix: Reuse one stored token per user.

blockers.symptom: 403 or 429 responses with rate limit headers.
blockers.cause: User tokens share 5,000 requests per hour, and secondary limits cap bursts.
blockers.fix: Move bulk reads to installation tokens, honor retry-after, and slow write bursts.

blockers.cause: GitHub suspended the app for abuse, spam, or API misuse.
blockers.fix: Check recent traffic for misuse and contact GitHub.

blockers.symptom: Authorization codes arrive at unexpected subdomains or paths.
blockers.cause: Apps with one callback URL from before Aug 3, 2026 have wildcard redirect matching on by default.
blockers.fix: Turn wildcard matching off on each callback URL unless you need it.

didForYou: Read about 19 official GitHub and Composio pages and cited each claim.
Probed the authorize endpoint with an invalid client ID. It is live and requires sign-in.
Checked github.com/settings/apps/new. It exists and needs sign-in.
Drafted an org owner request, a Marketplace description, and a permission rationale.
canDoForYou: Write PKCE sign-in, token storage, and refresh rotation.
Write the install check and redirect in onboarding.
Pick minimal permissions for your agent's actions.
Fill the GitHub App form in a browser after you sign in.
Draft privacy policy outline and Marketplace text.
youMustDo: Sign in to GitHub and pass 2FA.
Create the app, client secret, and private key.
Choose the owning account (personal or org).
Publish a privacy policy and support contact.
Accept the Marketplace Developer Agreement if you list.
Work with customer org owners on installs.

drafts.title: Org owner install request
drafts.body:
Hi <owner name>,

I want to use <App name> on our <org name> repositories. An owner must install it.

Access:
- Only repositories you select (for example <repo names>).
- Read: code, issues, pull requests, metadata.
- Write: issues and pull requests. It never pushes to protected branches.
- No organization permissions or repository administration.

Why: <one sentence on the task, for example "it triages new issues and opens fix PRs for us to review">.

Remove it any time under Organization settings, GitHub Apps. Install link: <https://github.com/apps/your-app/installations/new>
Privacy policy: <url>

Thanks,
<your name>

drafts.title: Marketplace listing description
drafts.body:
<App name> is a coding agent for repositories you choose. It reads code, issues, and pull requests, and proposes changes as pull requests.

What you control:
- Which repositories it sees.
- Minimal permissions: read code, read and write issues and pull requests.
- Nothing merges without a person.

Getting started: install, pick repositories, and sign in at <your site>.

Support: <support email or URL>. Privacy policy: <url>.

drafts.title: Permission rationale
drafts.body:
Metadata (read): required; lists visible repositories.
Contents (read): reads code to plan changes.
Contents (write): only to push PR branches.
Issues (read and write): reads, opens, and comments on issues.
Pull requests (read and write): opens PRs and replies to reviews.
Not requested: organization permissions, Repository administration, Workflows, so repo admins can install.

drafts.title: Privacy policy checklist
drafts.body:
- GitHub data read (code, issues, pull requests) and why.
- Which AI provider receives code, and whether it trains on it.
- Retention and deletion of code, tokens, and logs.
- How to revoke access and what happens to data.
- Storage location and who has access.
- Privacy contact email.

uncertainties.question: How long does Marketplace listing review take?
uncertainties.why: GitHub says an onboarding expert contacts you but gives no timeline.
uncertainties.howToResolve: Submit a free listing and record the dates, or ask GitHub Support.

uncertainties.question: Do enterprise policies change OAuth app restrictions or block GitHub App installs across an enterprise?
uncertainties.why: The pages read cover org-level controls only.
uncertainties.howToResolve: Read the Enterprise Cloud app policy docs, or ask an enterprise admin.

uncertainties.question: How long do org owners take to approve installs?
uncertainties.why: It varies by customer and no source gives a duration.
uncertainties.howToResolve: Track request-to-install time across beta customers.

uncertainties.question: What does a signed-in user see for an invalid client ID?
uncertainties.why: The signed-out probe hit the sign-in page before the client ID check.
uncertainties.howToResolve: Open the probe URL while signed in during setup and note the error.

evidence.claim: GitHub says GitHub Apps are generally preferred over OAuth apps. OAuth apps are still needed for enterprise-level resources, which GitHub Apps cannot get permissions for yet.
evidence.sourceTitle: Differences between GitHub Apps and OAuth apps

evidence.claim: GitHub Apps are not subject to organization application policies. When a policy is active, OAuth app access to the organization needs an owner's approval.
evidence.sourceTitle: Differences between GitHub Apps and OAuth apps

evidence.claim: A GitHub App only reaches the repositories chosen when it is installed. An OAuth app reaches everything the authorizing user can reach.
evidence.sourceTitle: Differences between GitHub Apps and OAuth apps

evidence.claim: Installing a GitHub App on an organization needs an organization owner or admin permission on a repository. Installation tokens expire after about one hour and act as a bot.
evidence.sourceTitle: Differences between GitHub Apps and OAuth apps

evidence.claim: OAuth apps support PKCE with code_challenge_method S256 only. GitHub strongly recommends it but does not require it.
Device flow must be enabled in the app settings first, or GitHub returns device_flow_disabled. Device codes expire after 15 minutes.
With wildcard matching off, redirect_uri must match a callback URL exactly. For loopback redirects the port may differ, and GitHub recommends 127.0.0.1 or ::1 over localhost.
Expiring user tokens last 8 hours and come with a refresh token that lasts 6 months. A refresh returns a new pair and the old refresh and access tokens stop working. Scopes cannot change on refresh.

GitHub keeps at most 10 tokens per user, app, and scope combination. Creating an 11th revokes one by a set order: never-used tokens first, then the least recently used. Token creation is also limited to 10 per hour per combination; past that, GitHub asks the user to re-authorize instead of revoking.
OAuth app access restrictions are enabled by default when you create a new organization. Members must then ask an owner to approve an OAuth app before it can reach organization resources.
evidence.note: Quote: "When you create a new organization, OAuth app access restrictions are enabled by default." The page gives no start date.

evidence.claim: A GitHub App user access token only has permissions that both the user and the app have. User tokens come from the web flow (PKCE S256 supported), device flow, or authorization during install, and expire after 8 hours with a 6 month refresh token.
evidence.sourceTitle: Generating a user access token for a GitHub App

evidence.claim: You register a GitHub App under Settings, Developer settings, GitHub Apps. The name is up to 34 characters and unique across GitHub. You can add up to 10 callback URLs. You choose whether the app installs only on your account or on any account. One account can own up to 100 GitHub Apps.
evidence.note: The page does not state form defaults. It tells you to deselect Expire user authorization tokens and webhook Active if you do not want them, and to select Enable Device Flow if you do, which implies tokens expire and webhooks are on by default and device flow is off.

evidence.claim: A public GitHub App can be installed and authorized by any GitHub user and can be listed on Marketplace. A private one installs only on the owning account, and only members of the owning org can authorize it.
evidence.sourceTitle: Making a GitHub App public or private

evidence.claim: Repository admins can install a third-party GitHub App in their org only if it requests no organization permissions and not Repository administration. Members and outside collaborators can request an install, and owners get notified. Installers choose all repositories or selected ones. Owners can block repo admins from installing apps, and then only an owner can install.
evidence.sourceTitle: Installing a GitHub App from a third party

evidence.claim: App access requests are enabled by default in organizations, so members and outside collaborators can request unapproved apps. Blocking requests from members is in public preview. If an owner both blocks requests and stops repo admins from installing apps, repo admins can neither install nor request.
evidence.sourceTitle: Limiting OAuth app and GitHub App access requests

evidence.claim: User tokens (personal tokens, OAuth app tokens, GitHub App user tokens) share 5,000 REST requests per hour per user. Installation tokens start at 5,000 and grow with repos and users up to 12,500, or 15,000 on Enterprise Cloud orgs.
evidence.sourceTitle: Rate limits for the REST API

evidence.claim: Secondary limits apply to all tokens: at most 100 concurrent requests, about 80 content-creating requests per minute and 500 per hour, and 2,000 OAuth token requests per hour per app.
evidence.sourceTitle: Rate limits for the REST API

evidence.claim: Anyone can list a free app on GitHub Marketplace. Only organization-owned apps whose org has completed publisher verification can sell paid plans.

Marketplace listings need a valid privacy policy link, a support link or email, value beyond authentication, a publicly available app, Marketplace webhook events, and acceptance of the Marketplace Developer Agreement. Paid listings need 100 installs for a GitHub App or 200 users for an OAuth app. No review timeline is given.

The repo scope grants full read and write access to public and private repositories. There is no read-only scope for private repository code. Users can edit granted scopes, so check the X-OAuth-Scopes header.

On Aug 14, 2026 GitHub let OAuth apps register up to 10 redirect URIs and use expiring tokens with refresh tokens, on by default for new apps or through the offline_access scope. It also made wildcard redirect matching visible and configurable per URI for OAuth apps and GitHub Apps.
evidence.sourceTitle: Changelog: multiple redirect URIs and token refresh for OAuth apps (Aug 14, 2026)

evidence.claim: Wildcard matching is set per callback URL. When on, any subdomain or subdirectory is accepted but the base host and port must match. Apps with a single callback URL from before Aug 3, 2026 have it on by default, and GitHub suggests turning it off if you do not need it.
evidence.sourceTitle: About the user authorization callback URL

evidence.claim: Authorization errors come back to your callback as error=application_suspended (contact GitHub Support), error=redirect_uri_mismatch, or error=access_denied.
GitHub Apps let you ask for read-only contents access instead of the write access the repo scope grants. Actions taken with a user token are labeled as the app acting for the user.
evidence.sourceTitle: Deciding when to build a GitHub App

evidence.claim: GitHub is in Composio's table of toolkits with Composio-managed OAuth available.
Reasons to bring your own app: your name on the consent screen, scopes beyond Composio's defaults, a dedicated rate limit instead of a shared one, and faster polling.
Existing connected accounts stay tied to the auth config they were created with. Switching to your own auth config affects only new connections.
The authorize endpoint is live. A signed-out request with an invalid client ID is redirected to the GitHub sign-in page, so the client ID is not checked before sign-in.
Developer portal: the new GitHub App form at github.com/settings/apps/new exists and needs a signed-in GitHub account.
For an agent that reads repos and opens issues and PRs for many users, a public GitHub App with user access tokens is the best fit.
evidence.note: GitHub prefers GitHub Apps (e1), they allow read-only contents (e24), limit access to chosen repos (e3), are exempt from OAuth app restrictions that are on by default in new orgs (e2, e10), and have refresh tokens by default (e12).

evidence.claim: How long an org owner takes to approve or install your app depends on each customer. GitHub gives no timeline, so the wait can range from minutes to never.
evidence.note: Owner approval is a customer decision (e10, e14, e15). No source gives a duration.

evidence.claim: When you request publication of a Marketplace listing, GitHub sends it for review and an onboarding expert contacts you. No timeline is given.

GitHub tells installers to make sure they trust an app's owner before installing it. Org owners can install apps, repo admins can install apps with no org permissions and no Repository administration, and owners can block repo admins from installing apps.
evidence.sourceTitle: Installing a GitHub App from GitHub Marketplace for your organizations

evidence.claim: Composio's GitHub toolkit uses OAuth2. You can bring your own GitHub App by adding its client ID and secret to the auth config. Users must still install the app and pick repositories, and Composio does not give them the install link, so you must.
